<ul class="glance-tags" aria-label="Scale and methods"><li>8 ERCOT weather zones</li><li>8,760 hours</li><li>9 scenarios</li><li>Two-stage stochastic LP</li><li>Inter-zonal hydrogen pipelines</li></ul>

<section class="proj-q" aria-labelledby="h-question">
<h2 id="h-question"><i class="bi bi-question-circle" aria-hidden="true"></i>Research question</h2>
<p class="proj-question">Where should electrolyzers, hydrogen storage and fuel cells be built in ERCOT, and how should hydrogen move between zones, to absorb surplus renewable generation and supply industrial hydrogen demand under uncertain 2030 renewable build-out?</p>
</section>
<section class="proj-insight" id="insight" aria-labelledby="h-insight">
<h2 id="h-insight"><i class="bi bi-stars" aria-hidden="true"></i>Key insight</h2>
<p class="insight-title">Dearer gas power diverted green hydrogen to power generation and raised emissions</p>
<p>When gas-fired backup power became much more expensive, the model built fuel cells and turned stored green hydrogen back into electricity. Industry then drew more hydrogen from gas reformers, and the round trip from power to hydrogen and back lost energy, so total emissions rose although gas-plant emissions fell.</p>
</section>
<section class="proj-sec proj-explainer" id="explainer" aria-labelledby="h-explainer">
<h2 id="h-explainer"><i class="bi bi-sliders" aria-hidden="true"></i>How can dearer gas power raise emissions?</h2>
<div class="explainer" data-explainer="txh2">
<p class="ex-fallback">When gas-fired backup power becomes more expensive, the model starts to use stored green hydrogen in fuel cells to make electricity in hours of low wind and sun. That hydrogen no longer supplies industry, so gas reformers fill the gap with fossil hydrogen. Converting electricity to hydrogen and back loses energy, so in the paper&#x27;s high-price cases total emissions rose even though emissions from gas plants fell.</p>
</div>
<p class="ex-note"><i class="bi bi-info-circle" aria-hidden="true"></i>Illustrative model with stylized numbers: it shows the mechanism described in the paper, not the study&#x27;s data or results.</p>
</section>
<script src="../assets/explainers/common.js" defer></script>
<script src="../assets/explainers/txh2.js" defer></script>
<section class="proj-sec" aria-labelledby="h-contribution">
<h2 id="h-contribution"><i class="bi bi-person-check" aria-hidden="true"></i>My contribution</h2>
<p>First author. I did most of the work: the data pipeline from public ERCOT market disclosures, the stochastic planning model, the analysis and the writing.</p>
</section>
<section class="proj-sec" id="approach" aria-labelledby="h-approach">
<h2 id="h-approach"><i class="bi bi-tools" aria-hidden="true"></i>How I approached it</h2>
<ol class="approach">
<li class="ap-card"><p class="ap-challenge"><span class="ap-k">Challenge</span>The model needed hourly wind and solar output for each of ERCOT&#x27;s eight weather zones.</p><p class="ap-did"><span class="ap-k">What I did</span>I built it from ERCOT&#x27;s 60-day market disclosures: each wind and solar resource mapped to its county and zone, averaged to hours, gap-filled and summed, then turned into zone capacity factors.</p><p class="ap-why"><span class="ap-k">Why it mattered</span>The same capacity factors scaled planned capacity from the interconnection queue, so existing and future renewables shared one hourly basis.</p></li>
<li class="ap-card"><p class="ap-challenge"><span class="ap-k">Challenge</span>How much planned renewable capacity is built by 2030, and how fast demand grows, are both uncertain.</p><p class="ap-did"><span class="ap-k">What I did</span>I formulated a two-stage stochastic program: hydrogen equipment is sized once, then operated hour by hour in nine scenarios combining three completion rates and three demand levels.</p><p class="ap-why"><span class="ap-k">Why it mattered</span>The sizes minimize expected cost over all nine scenarios instead of fitting a single forecast.</p></li>
<li class="ap-card"><p class="ap-challenge"><span class="ap-k">Challenge</span>Wind and solar output is concentrated far from electricity demand in the north and southeast, and from hydrogen demand on the Gulf Coast.</p><p class="ap-did"><span class="ap-k">What I did</span>I added hydrogen pipelines between adjacent weather zones, with transport cost set by the distance between zone centres.</p><p class="ap-why"><span class="ap-k">Why it mattered</span>The model could then choose between making hydrogen near surplus power and moving it, or making it where it is used.</p></li>
</ol>
</section>
<section class="proj-sec" id="choices" aria-labelledby="h-choices">
<h2 id="h-choices"><i class="bi bi-signpost-split" aria-hidden="true"></i>Design choices</h2>
<dl class="choices">
<div class="choice"><dt>Hold hydrogen demand fixed across scenarios</dt><dd><span class="ch-alt">Alternatives considered: treating hydrogen demand as a third uncertain factor</span>Reliable hydrogen-demand data were lacking and computational cost mattered; the paper names this as future work.</dd></div>
<div class="choice"><dt>Move hydrogen only by pipeline between neighbouring zones</dt><dd><span class="ch-alt">Alternatives considered: adding truck or rail transport</span>Pipelines are the relevant mode for large-scale, long-term deployment; other modes were left out to keep the focus on supply and demand uncertainty.</dd></div>
</dl>
</section>
<section class="proj-sec" aria-labelledby="h-method">
<h2 id="h-method"><i class="bi bi-diagram-3" aria-hidden="true"></i>Method</h2>
<p>Two-stage stochastic linear program. The first stage sizes electrolyzers, hydrogen tanks and fuel cells in each of ERCOT&#x27;s eight weather zones; the second stage schedules batteries, electrolysis, fuel cells, gas-fired backup, reformer hydrogen and inter-zonal hydrogen transport hour by hour over a full year, in nine scenarios (three electricity-demand levels by three completion rates of planned renewable capacity). Inputs are built from ERCOT 60-day SCED disclosures, the LBNL interconnection queue and EIA data.</p>
</section>
<section class="proj-sec" aria-labelledby="h-findings">
<h2 id="h-findings"><i class="bi bi-lightbulb" aria-hidden="true"></i>Key findings</h2>
<ol class="findings">
<li>Renewable (green) hydrogen covered only a few percent of industrial hydrogen demand; reformer hydrogen remained the main supply.</li>
<li>Modest load flexibility (±5%) reduced CO₂ emissions from combined-cycle gas generation.</li>
</ol>
</section>
<section class="proj-sec proj-bounds" aria-labelledby="h-bounds">
<h2 id="h-bounds"><i class="bi bi-exclamation-circle" aria-hidden="true"></i>Boundary conditions</h2>
<p>Inputs reflect 2022–2023 conditions; post-2023 federal hydrogen credit rules are not modeled.</p>
</section>

<h2 id="h-next"><i class="bi bi-arrow-right-circle" aria-hidden="true"></i>What it led to</h2>

</section>
